text:
At this point, I don't see any scenario where Joey Porter Jr. plays a snap for the Steelers this season until *at least* Week 10 after the NFL trade deadline has passed.

Because of that, I think Steelers GM Omar Khan currently has 2 choices in how to handle the Joey Porter Jr. situation in the weeks to come: ⬇️

Choice #1: Trade Joey for a good return of future draft capital before the deadline passes this year on November 10th. I would consider this the 'safe' option for PIT, especially if you can get a legitimately good return for him.

Choice #2: Don't trade Joey before the deadline & hope he plays out the final 9 games of the year  + (hopefully) playoffs once he knows he can't be traded for the rest of the season, where you can then take long-term contract negotiations into the 2027 offseason with the franchise tag in your back pocket after Porter hopefully plays well in the 2nd half of the year.

I think Choice #2 is riskier for the Steelers because if Joey decides to not play the entire season, PIT is risking losing Porter next offseason (because I don't think PIT is offering a player that just sat out an entire season a fully guaranteed $23 million dollar franchise tag) for a return of just a mid-round comp pick in 2028 when you could have traded him for much more that that before the trade deadline this season.

With that said, Choice #2 is the only realistic pathway I can see that potentially results in a long-term contract getting done for JPJ here in Pittsburgh, so if that's still the goal and/or PIT doesn't get any good trade offers for Porter in the weeks to come, I could see Omar take that risk.

Either way, I think we're looking at Asante Samuel Jr. as PIT's other starting CB opposite Jamel Dean for *at least* the next 7 games. 

Thank God the easier portion of the Steelers' schedule comes before the trade deadline this year...

Patrick Graham’s first game running the Steelers defense offered a pretty clear glimpse of what he wants this unit to become.

T.J. Watt moved around the formation. Pittsburgh generated pressure without needing to blitz heavily. The outside linebackers rotated more often, and Watt and Alex Highsmith still had plenty left when the fourth quarter arrived.

That flexibility may be the biggest takeaway.

Graham isn’t interested in building a defense around one coverage, one pressure package or even one position for some of his best players. He wants offenses guessing where Watt is coming from, how Nick Herbig will be used and whether Pittsburgh is bringing pressure at all.

Week 1 showed just how dangerous that approach can be.

Watt finished with two sacks, multiple tackles for loss and a pick-six, while the rest of the defense consistently made life difficult for Atlanta.

And according to Graham, this is only the beginning of how he plans to “weaponize” the talent on Pittsburgh’s defense.

BREAKING: FIFTH CIRCUIT KILLS FEDERAL BAN ON INTERSTATE HANDGUN SALES

A Federal Appeals Court Struck Down A Longstanding Ban On Buying Handguns Across State Lines Today. The Fifth Circuit Ruled The Ban Violates The Second Amendment. The Court Reversed A Texas District Court & Entered Judgment For The Gun Owners Who Sued.

The Law At Issue Is Part Of 18 U.S.C. § 922. It Stops A Licensed Gun Shop In One State From Selling A Handgun Directly To A Buyer Who Lives In Another State. Rifles & Shotguns Can Be Sold Across State Lines If Both States’ Rules Are Followed. Handguns Cannot. Buyers Must Route The Gun Through A Second Licensed Shop In Their Home State. That Extra Step Often Costs $30 To $40 Plus Extra Delay.

Elite Precision Customs, A Licensed Shop In Mansfield, Texas, Wanted To Sell Handguns Straight To Out-Of-State Customers. Tim Herron Of Arizona & Freddie Blish Of New Mexico Said They Would Buy From That Shop If The Ban Did Not Exist. Firearms Policy Coalition Joined The Suit.

Judge Jerry E. Smith Wrote The Majority Opinion. Judges Smith & Engelhardt Formed The Majority. Judge Haynes Dissented.

The Court Applied The Supreme Court’s Bruen Test. Step One Asks Whether The Conduct Falls Under The Second Amendment’s Plain Text. The Court Said Yes. The Right To Keep Arms Includes The Right To Buy Them. A Law That Blocks An Entire Class Of Lawful Handgun Purchases Hits That Text. The Ban Is Therefore Presumed Unconstitutional.

Step Two Requires The Government To Prove The Ban Matches The Nation’s Historical Tradition Of Firearm Regulation. The Government Offered Old Colonial & Early-State Laws About Wartime Sales, Sales To Indian Tribes, Gunpowder Inspection, & Product Quality Rules. The Court Said Those Laws Do Not Match. They Concern War, Foreign Borders, Or Product Safety. They Do Not Justify A Peacetime Ban On Handgun Sales Between States By Peaceable People.

The Court Also Rejected The Claim That The Extra Shop-To-Shop Transfer Saves The Ban. The Direct Sale Remains Completely Forbidden. No Waiting Period Turns An Illegal Sale Into A Legal One. Forcing People To Pay Extra Fees To Use A Basic Right Raised Separate Concern.

The Fifth Circuit Explicitly Rejected A Contrary Ruling From The Second Circuit That Upheld The Same Ban. That Creates A Split Between Appeals Courts.

The Mandate Is Set To Issue November 9, 2026. The Ruling Does Not Change Other Federal Gun Laws Such As Background Checks.

Source: United States Court Of Appeals For The Fifth Circuit, Elite Precision Customs V. ATF, No. 25-11206, Filed September 18, 2026.

🇺🇸🧠 Scientists integrate human brain tissue into mice

Stanford researchers grew human cortical organoids from reprogrammed cells and transplanted them into mice engineered to lack much of their cerebral cortex. The human tissue expanded to fill more than 90 percent of the available space and formed connections with mouse neurons, including projections reaching the spinal cord. The advance gives scientists a way to observe developing human cells inside a living nervous system and investigate conditions such as epilepsy, autism and schizophrenia. It also provides something isolated cell cultures cannot, the interaction between human tissue, neural circuits and behavior. At the same time, this level of integration raises added ethical questions and makes careful monitoring of the animals increasingly important. The model offers a more biologically complete research setting, but it remains a laboratory model rather than a human brain.

What Can We Reflect Upon After Reading the Story of Zen Master Hakuin?

In today’s rapidly developing age of big data, the pace of life continues to accelerate, while competition and pressure increase along with it. Driven by ever-growing greed and desires, many people resort to deception, fabrication, slander, and defamation.

So when disputes, lies, and deception actually confront us, how should we respond to them properly?

The Story of Zen Master Hakuin

There is a well-known Zen story:

Zen Master Hakuin was an eminent monk renowned for his strict observance of the precepts and was deeply respected by the people around him.

What Can We Reflect Upon After Reading the Story of Zen Master Hakuin?
Near the temple where Zen Master Hakuin lived was a family with an unmarried daughter who became pregnant. When her parents discovered her pregnancy, they were furious and repeatedly demanded to know who the father of the child was. Under intense pressure from her parents, the daughter finally uttered the name, “Hakuin.”

Shocked and enraged, her parents gathered a group of people and stormed into the temple. In front of everyone, they humiliated Zen Master Hakuin and even beat him.

Yet Zen Master Hakuin offered no explanation or defense. He simply responded softly:

“Is that so?”

After the baby was born, the girl’s parents carried the child to the temple, left the baby with Zen Master Hakuin, and departed while angrily cursing him.

As news of the scandal spread, public outrage erupted. People accused Zen Master Hakuin of being a hypocrite. Some spat at him, insulted him, and even threw stones at him. As the saying goes, “Good news travels slowly, but bad news travels fast.” Before long, Zen Master Hakuin’s reputation was ruined.

Yet no matter how severely he was insulted, he silently endured everything without defending himself or arguing. Every day, he carried the infant with him and went from place to place seeking milk and other necessities for the child.

Eventually, the young woman could no longer bear the guilt and condemnation weighing upon her conscience. She finally confessed the truth to her parents: the actual father of the child was a young man who sold fish.

After learning the truth, the parents and their daughter went to the temple filled with profound shame and respect. They apologized to Zen Master Hakuin, expressed their remorse, and asked to take the child back.

Zen Master Hakuin remained just as composed as he had been at the beginning, as though nothing had ever happened. As he handed the child back to them, he simply said softly:

“Is that so?”

Zen Master Hakuin was indeed an eminent monk of genuine virtue. When he was falsely accused, personally humiliated, condemned as though he had committed an unforgivable offense, and stripped of his reputation, he neither defended himself nor argued or tried to justify himself. Instead, he continued to place the well-being of living beings before himself.

Amid insults, humiliation, and condemnation, he continued to care attentively for the child. Throughout the entire ordeal, he maintained compassion and patiently endured the tremendous humiliation and hardship placed upon him.

What Can We Learn From This Story?

Now that the story has been told, what can we deeply reflect upon?

In Philosophical Sayings on Worldly Matters, Namo H.H. Dorje Chang Buddha III taught:

In a dispute about right and wrong, there is nothing worse than to stick to one’s position and continue arguing, thus compounding one’s wrong and finally getting into trouble. For this reason, one should not let oneself be overwhelmed by disputes.

The general meaning of this teaching is that when we encounter slander or ridicule, we should not hold it in our hearts. As time passes, such disputes will naturally and gradually fade away because their very nature is impermanent. Therefore, when confronted with disputes over right and wrong, not holding them in our hearts benefits both ourselves and others.

In real life, when we actually encounter disputes, lies, slander, defamation, or other malicious tactics, if we respond with hatred, anger, insults, or emotional outbursts, ultimately we are the ones who suffer. Our anger, hatred, and verbal outbursts may not harm the other person in the slightest; the other person may even secretly take pleasure in seeing us become upset. If instead we choose retaliation, what we receive in return may simply be even stronger retaliation.

Therefore, in learning Buddhism and cultivating ourselves, we must conscientiously practice in accordance with the teachings of Namo H.H. Dorje Chang Buddha III. We should understand that all matters and phenomena are inseparable from cause and effect. We should learn to put ourselves in others’ shoes, be tolerant toward others, maintain compassion, patiently endure adversity and humiliation, and refrain from holding disputes over right and wrong in our hearts.

If we can do so, not only will we avoid being overwhelmed by pressure, conflict, and disputes, but we will also be able to temper and strengthen ourselves through difficulties and challenges.

Zen Master Hakuin provides a powerful example. Amid disputes, humiliation, and false accusations, he patiently endured and continued his cultivation. Rather than being swayed by external circumstances, his conduct revealed even more clearly the virtue and dignity of a truly eminent monk.

The path of life must be walked by each of us, one step at a time. Which path we choose to follow is ultimately our own choice.

When we can truly understand cause and effect and awaken to the truth of impermanence, we can gain deeper insight into life. In doing so, we can better make use of this precious lifetime and ultimately walk toward a life filled with happiness, brightness, and hope.

Some ultra-Orthodox Jews in New York have been performing kapparot (also spelled kaporos) in the days before Yom Kippur. That is the custom people saw: live chickens waved over people’s heads, then slaughtered. To many outsiders it looks brutal. The timing this year fits: Yom Kippur 2026 begins at sundown on Sunday, September 20.

Here is what the ritual actually is.

Kapparot is not a commandment in the Torah or the Talmud. It first appears in Jewish sources around the 9th century. A person takes a live chicken—usually a rooster for a man, a hen for a woman—swings it three times over the head, and recites words to the effect of: “This is my exchange, this is my substitute, this is my atonement. This bird will go to death, and I will enter a good, long life and peace.” The bird is then killed according to kosher slaughter rules and, in theory, given to the poor. Many communities use money instead and give it to charity. The practice is concentrated among certain Hasidic and other Haredi groups, especially in Brooklyn neighborhoods such as Crown Heights, Williamsburg, and Borough Park. Tens of thousands of chickens are used in New York each year. Plenty of other Jews reject the live-animal version as cruel, unsanitary, and unnecessary.

It is a folk custom meant to picture substitution and repentance before the Day of Atonement. It is not the Temple sacrificial system of Leviticus. Those sacrifices ended when the Temple was destroyed in A.D. 70.

From a Christian reading of Scripture, that is the larger point. The Law’s sacrificial system pointed forward. Hebrews says those offerings could never take away sins; they were shadows. Jesus is presented as the one who fulfilled them: the once-for-all atonement. People who do not receive that fulfillment are left trying to cover guilt by ritual, charity, fasting, and good works.

That is where Isaiah 64:6 lands:

All of us have become like one who is unclean,  
and all our righteous acts are like filthy rags;  
we all shrivel up like a leaf,  
and like the wind our sins sweep us away.

The Hebrew behind “filthy rags” (beged iddim) is graphic. It refers to a cloth stained by menstrual blood—something Leviticus treated as ritually unclean. Isaiah is not saying kindness is worthless. He is saying that when people offer their own righteousness as the thing that makes them acceptable to God, it does not cover them. It is defiled. It cannot stand before a holy God.

So the shock many people feel watching kapparot is real. The deeper claim in your original point is this: waving a chicken, giving money, keeping festivals, or piling up religious works cannot do what only a perfect substitute can do. In Christian theology, that substitute is Christ. Without Him, the old pattern of trying to reach heaven by works remains—and Isaiah’s verdict on those works is still the same.

South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung declared on September 18 that Seoul will not deploy troops or military assets to support U.S.-led operations against Iran. The language was unambiguous: "There won't be deployment that would involve or enter war. I can tell you that very clearly. We won't deploy military assets in any form to that end."

This is assessed with a high validation process as a deliberate, domestically anchored strategic choice — not a negotiating posture or temporary diplomatic hedge.

The domestic math makes reversal politically expensive. A Pew Research Center survey from spring 2026 found 55% of South Koreans hold an unfavorable view of the United States — up from 39% in 2025 and a 35-point drop from 2018, near an all-time low. That number gives Lee political cover that is unlikely to shift before the next election cycle.

Washington has already applied coercive pressure. The Trump administration scaled back Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises in August, explicitly linking the cut to Seoul's refusal to join Iran-related operations. The available evidence suggests this approach is producing diminishing returns: each coercive act raises Seoul's domestic cost of compliance rather than lowering it.

Lee's offer to expand Cheonghae maritime operations near the Strait of Hormuz appears calibrated as a minimum contribution to forestall further U.S. retaliation — not a strategic pivot toward war participation. His language explicitly limits any Hormuz role to protecting commercial shipping and the safety of South Korean nationals.

Two compounding dynamics deserve attention, both assessed at moderate confidence.

North Korea conducted 24 ballistic missile tests since Trump returned to office, including one just days before the exercise reduction announcement. The alliance fracture may be creating a window that Pyongyang is actively exploiting — a risk neither capital appears to be addressing coherently.

China is also moving. Wang Yi visited Seoul on August 19–20, and Beijing's patient reorientation strategy gains traction each time Washington's pressure reinforces the perception that the alliance is transactional rather than mutual.

The structural tension here is real: U.S. efforts to leverage the Korean alliance for Iran coalition-building may be weakening the very deterrent architecture that justifies American forward presence on the peninsula.

Good try John.  Your argument conflates rejecting a bad deal with walking away from the U.S. market. Canada can do the former without doing the latter.  Let’s not mix things up.

Yes, the U.S. remains Canada’s largest export market. So far in 2026 about 65% of exports went south,   In 2025, about 72% of Canadian merchandise exports went to the U.S. — down from 76% in 2024.   Notice a trend?  If not look at the chart.   Within 5 years exports are expected to decline to 50% of overall trade.  Still quite substantial but diversification is in full swing.  

Canada will never accept whatever terms Washington offers unless it’s a fair deal.  Most Americans simply do not understand that over 70% of Canadians support “no deal”.

And the claim that Canada “cannot” sell elsewhere is already contradicted by the data. In 2025, Canadian exports to non-U.S. markets rose 17.2%, while exports to the U.S. fell 5.8%. In Q1 2026, the U.S. share of Canada’s total goods-and-services exports had fallen to 64.1%, the lowest since this series began. 

Nor is energy permanently trapped in the U.S. market. The Trans Mountain expansion increased capacity from 300,000 to 890,000 barrels/day and created direct Pacific access.  More pipelines and infrastructure are planned.   In 2025, Canada exported substantially more crude to the Indo-Pacific, with China becoming the leading buyer of TMX seaborne shipments.

Drop the false choice with Europe. Nobody seriously argues that an undefined EU “associate membership” suddenly replaces the American market. It doesn’t. However,  Canada already has CETA, and EU-Canada trade is growing. In 2025, Canadian exports to the EU increased 23.5% for goods and 5.8% for services, reaching $67.7 billion in total exports. CETA is already provisionally in force and eliminates duties on 99% of tariff lines; Yes, 10 EU states still have to complete ratification. 

Criticizing the proposed “associate membership” as unfinished is fair. But that does not establish that Canada has no alternatives. The EU proposal is one piece of a broader diversification strategy, not a replacement for the U.S. overnight.    The proposal itself is still undefined and would require further negotiations.

“Every month spent selling an undefined European status as the alternative is a month the next American offer gets worse.”

Dream on.   There is no evidence presented for that causal claim.

A negotiation isn’t a choice between accepting today’s American terms and having no customers. Canada can maintain existing U.S. trade, challenge tariffs where appropriate, expand other markets, build export infrastructure and negotiate from a position in which dependence on one customer gradually decreases.

That’s precisely why “no deal is better than a bad deal” can make economic sense: the alternative to a bad deal isn’t necessarily no trade — it can be continued trade under existing arrangements while working to improve alternatives, building critical infrastructure and making new trade deals.  It will take time.  One thing for sure the US/Canada relationship will never return to what it was.
